profiles.meeting_scenario: At a large NHS cancer centre, the Enhanced Supportive Care (ESC) service is preparing to extend its model into the lung and upper GI pathways ahead of the next reporting cycle to the divisional cancer board. This 30-minute coordination meeting is between the ESC clinical lead and the oncology operations lead to align the weekly MDT handoff, the shared patient list, the two-week access KPI, and who handles downstream follow-up booking. The immediate trigger is that board reporting starts next Monday, and both teams want a low-friction process that fits existing systems without slowing referrals. The agenda is to confirm what data will be circulated before Thursday MDT, how the two-week target will be tracked, what status numbers will be submitted to the board, and how follow-up actions will move between ESC and oncology scheduling teams. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the handoff process, tracking approach, and booking workflow so rollout can begin on Monday, even though several second-order assumptions remain quietly misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
members.role: Consultant in Palliative Medicine and Clinical Lead for Enhanced Supportive Care
members.expertise: Early palliative care integration, symptom control, treatment-side effect management, outpatient ESC pathway design
members.background: Aisha has led the trust's supportive care clinic for three years and helped broaden it from a mainly early palliative care offer into a wider ESC model supporting patients on active treatment as well as selected survivors with ongoing symptom burden.
members.private_state: She wants the expansion to show that ESC is a clinically meaningful service with direct patient assessment and continuity, and she worries that if reporting is built around administrative throughput the service will be recast as a lightweight triage layer rather than specialist care.
hidden_assumptions: When leadership asks for ESC activity numbers, the reporting clock should start only once an ESC clinician has made substantive patient contact and documented an assessment or management plan.
The 'ESC list' is the curated live worksheet held by the ESC CNS team, because it is the only version that reflects symptom complexity, actual contacts, and planned reviews.
The two-week target is evidence of early patient access, so it only counts if the patient has had a patient-facing review or a direct clinician call that results in active management.
After the first ESC clinical review, onward follow-up belongs operationally to ESC unless a deliberate discharge back to oncology has been made.

members.name: Tom Bennett
members.expertise: Cancer pathway operations, MDT coordination, performance reporting, outpatient capacity planning
members.background: Tom oversees operational delivery across several solid tumour services and has been asked to spread ESC trust-wide by embedding it into existing oncology tracking, booking, and board-reporting mechanisms rather than creating a parallel administrative structure.
members.private_state: He needs the rollout to look orderly, scalable, and measurable from day one, and he is concerned that bespoke clinical nuances will create extra admin work, reduce visible uptake, and make it harder to defend clinic capacity at the cancer board.
hidden_assumptions: For board and pathway reporting, the clock starts when a referral is accepted onto the tracker, because that is when the service has formally taken responsibility for the patient.
The 'ESC list' is the standard oncology tracker extract circulated before MDT, since named lists used for cross-team coordination should come from the central operational source of truth.
The two-week target is a throughput KPI, so it is met once ESC has triaged, reviewed notes, or otherwise dispositioned the referral within two weeks, even if the actual appointment is later.
Once ESC advises frequency after the first review, routine booking should sit with existing oncology scheduling staff unless the patient is being seen in a ring-fenced ESC clinic.

misalignment_points.topic: When the reporting clock starts for ESC numbers
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they can start reporting ESC uptake from Monday and that the board needs a clean weekly number.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the reported count should include only patients who have actually had an ESC clinical assessment or direct management contact, because that is when ESC activity truly begins.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the reported count should include referrals accepted onto the ESC tracker from Monday onward, because that is the operational start of the pathway.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The discussion is framed around board reporting logistics and having a 'clean number,' which makes the phrase feel like a routine counting convention rather than a substantive definition; both assume their own start-point is the obvious one used in NHS reporting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to updating and circulating 'the ESC list' before the Thursday MDT.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the ESC team's live worksheet that includes symptom issues, whether contact has actually occurred, and planned review actions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the filtered oncology tracker extract showing accepted referrals, dates, and booking status.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The patient names overlap heavily and both artifacts are used in adjacent weekly routines, so 'the ESC list' sounds perfectly adequate; each participant assumes the other means the familiar list already central to their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the service should be hitting the two-week target for new ESC referrals.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the target is met only when the patient has received a genuine ESC clinical review, such as a consultation or direct management call, within two weeks of referral.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the target is met when ESC has clinically triaged or dispositioned the referral within two weeks, even if the patient-facing appointment occurs later or is deemed unnecessary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'two-week target' is treated as an established KPI, so attention naturally shifts to whether it is achievable rather than what event completes it; because both endorse timely access, the hidden threshold difference feels too minor to unpack in a coordination call.

misalignment_points.topic: Who actually books follow-up after first review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'we'll just book follow-up from the first review' so patients keep moving through the pathway.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes ESC clinicians or ESC admin will directly arrange and own the next appointment after the first ESC review, unless the patient is discharged.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes oncology booking staff will place the follow-up based on ESC instructions, using existing tumour-pathway scheduling processes, with ESC only specifying timing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The wording uses an unexamined collective 'we' and presents follow-up booking as downstream routine administration; because both teams already have habitual local processes, each silently maps the shared plan onto their own standard method.

turns.inner_thought: I need this launch to land as a real clinical service, not an administrative shadow of one. If reporting starts Monday, the uptake number should only begin once one of us has actually assessed the patient or had a direct management conversation and documented it. Otherwise the board will think volume equals care, and ESC will be reduced to a holding pen.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Tom. I mainly want to make sure lung and upper GI go live cleanly on Monday, especially with the first cancer board return in the same week. If we keep it simple from the outset, we can start reporting ESC uptake from Monday and give the board a clean weekly number.

turns.inner_thought: Good — that's exactly the kind of operational framing I need. From Monday I can count accepted referrals on the tracker and show immediate uptake. I also need one stable list before MDT and a straightforward way to show we're meeting the two-week KPI without building a separate reporting universe around ESC.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. From my side, the main things are a stable list before MDT, a straightforward weekly number for the board, and a practical way to show we're tracking the two-week target for new ESC referrals.

turns.inner_thought: Our CNS worksheet is the only list that really shows what matters clinically — who has actually been contacted, what symptoms are emerging, and what reviews are planned. And the two-week target should reflect genuine patient access. Once we've done a first proper review, the onward follow-up should sit with ESC unless we've consciously discharged the patient back.
turns.utterance: That all sounds fine. We can update the ESC list before Thursday so the MDT can see who has been contacted, the kinds of issues coming through, and what reviews are planned. And from the clinical side, we should be hitting the two-week target for new referrals. After the first review, we'll just book follow-up from there so patients keep moving through the pathway.

turns.inner_thought: Great — as long as the ESC list is the standard tracker extract, we're aligned. I want one shared operational version circulated before MDT, not a separate clinically curated sheet that creates reconciliation work. If that goes out Wednesday afternoon, everyone can work off the same source.
turns.utterance: Perfect. As long as the ESC list goes round before Thursday, that should keep everybody lined up for MDT.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep nudging toward meaning without turning this into a definitional debate. The board numbers need to reflect early ESC input in a way that demonstrates patient benefit and specialist involvement, not just administrative movement through a pathway.
turns.utterance: Exactly. The main thing for me is that the board figures say something meaningful about patients getting early ESC input, not just that the process has started.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed, and we can still show momentum straight away by counting from the point the pathway formally starts. That gives the board an immediate visible uptake line while clinic utilisation settles, which is what I need to defend capacity.
turns.utterance: Completely. If we start from Monday, we'll be able to show uptake straight away, which will help demonstrate momentum while things bed in.

turns.inner_thought: The point of the two-week standard is timely support before toxicity, distress, and treatment disruption build up. I assume that's obvious; there shouldn't be any need to spell out that this means an actual ESC clinical review rather than internal handling.
turns.utterance: Yes. And clinically the whole point of the two-week target is that people get support early, before toxicity or distress has a chance to escalate.

turns.inner_thought: That KPI should be manageable if the team can process and disposition referrals inside two weeks even when appointment capacity is tight. I don't need to say that out loud; as long as we can evidence the target consistently, the board will be satisfied.
turns.utterance: I think that should be manageable. Even when capacity is tight, we should still be able to keep the two-week target on track.

turns.inner_thought: Continuity is crucial. Once ESC has done the first review, I expect the service to own follow-up operationally unless we've discharged the patient. Otherwise they'll drift back into oncology admin and the model will lose coherence.
turns.utterance: Good. And after the first review, we'll just book follow-up from there so patients aren't bouncing around unnecessarily.

turns.inner_thought: Fine — in practice that can sit neatly in the existing oncology booking flow once ESC indicates timing and slot type. No need to create a separate admin setup unless we're dealing with ring-fenced ESC clinic space.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. As long as that's built in from the first review, it should keep people moving through the pathway.

turns.inner_thought: I also want the board to see symptom burden and repeat contacts, otherwise ESC will look like a one-touch throughput line. The early reporting needs enough clinical texture to show this is specialist assessment and ongoing management.
turns.utterance: For the board return, I'd also like the numbers to sit alongside the common symptom themes and any repeat contacts, so the clinical value is visible early rather than it being just a headline figure.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable. I'll set the tracker fields so we can produce the board number cleanly, use the standard tracker extract as the ESC list before MDT, and start the Monday count from the point patients are accepted onto the pathway. That gives me a scalable process from day one.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. I'll align the tracker fields, make sure the ESC list goes out before MDT, and start the Monday count for the weekly board report so we've got a clean run into next week.
